cards.biological_mechanism: Complete girdling interrupts basipetal phloem transport of photosynthates and polar auxin (IAA). Auxin and carbohydrate accumulation at the upper girdle margin triggers dedifferentiation of phloem/cambial parenchyma into adventitious root primordia under darkness, moisture, and aeration.
cards.horticultural_practice: Practiced during the humid monsoon season on woody branches. A 2.5-4 cm ring of bark and cambium is scraped clean, treated with rooting powder (IBA 1000-2500 ppm), enclosed in moist sphagnum moss, and tightly sealed with 200-gauge polyethylene film tied at both ends.
cards.exam_trap: Do NOT confuse with ground layering: air layering is performed in situ on upright, elevated, rigid woody branches that cannot be bent to ground level. Girdling must thoroughly scrape the cambium to prevent healing callus from bridging the wound instead of rooting.
cards.key_crops: Litchi (Litchi chinensis), Guava (Psidium guajava), Pomegranate (Punica granatum), Ficus elastica
cards.notes: Essential propagation technique for true-to-type litchi cultivars in Bangladesh.
cards.etymology: Compound term from Middle English 'air' (via Old French from Greek ἀήρ, 'aēr', atmosphere) and 'layering' (from Middle English 'leyere', an established shoot laid down for rooting, from Old English 'lecgan', to lay).
cards.synonyms: marcottage, Chinese layering, pot layering
cards.see_also: layering, adventitious roots, girdling, sphagnum moss, clonal propagation

cards.biological_mechanism: Asexual seed formation (agamospermy) bypassing female meiosis (apomeiosis) and egg fertilization (parthenogenesis). Occurs via gametophytic apomixis (diplospory or apospory forming unreduced embryo sacs) or sporophytic adventitious embryony directly from somatic nucellus/integument cells.
cards.horticultural_practice: Commercial citrus breeders exploit natural nucellar polyembryony in rootstocks (e.g. Rangpur lime, Rough lemon) to mass-propagate uniform, clonal, virus-free rootstock seedlings from seed, drastically cutting nursery grafting costs.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Apomixis produces clonal SEEDS without fertilization; Parthenocarpy produces SEEDLESS FRUIT without fertilization. Furthermore, apospory is only one sub-pathway of apomixis, not a synonym.
cards.key_crops: Citrus spp. (Rangpur lime, Sweet orange), Mangifera indica (polyembryonic mangoes), Poa pratensis (Kentucky bluegrass)
cards.notes: Natural heterosis fixator in plant breeding.
cards.etymology: Coined in 1908 by German botanist Hans Winkler from Greek ἀπό ('apo-', without/away from) and μῖξις ('mixis', mingling or sexual union).
cards.synonyms: agamospermy
cards.see_also: parthenogenesis, apospory, diplospory, adventitious embryony, polyembryony, parthenocarpy

cards.biological_mechanism: The biological subdiscipline evaluating the physiological, biochemical, and physical mechanisms by which horticultural crops dynamically acclimate and respond to abiotic environmental gradients (solar irradiance, vapor pressure deficit, temperature extremes, drought stress, and soil salinity). Investigates stomatal conductance regulation, leaf gas exchange, water-use efficiency (WUE), and photosynthetic quantum yield (chlorophyll fluorescence Fv/Fm).
cards.horticultural_practice: Applied in orchard canopy management and precision deficit irrigation (RDI) for high-density fruit orchards (mango, citrus, guava). Portable infrared gas analyzers (LI-COR) and porometers are used to quantify stomatal conductance and transpiration rates to optimize irrigation intervals and prevent midday photoinhibition.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT confuse phenotypic ecophysiological acclimation (reversible, physiological adjustments like stomatal closure, leaf rolling, or osmoprotectant synthesis occurring within an individual plant lifespan) with evolutionary adaptation (heritable, genetic changes across generations). Furthermore, high atmospheric vapor pressure deficit (VPD) can induce midday stomatal closure even when soil moisture is at field capacity!
cards.key_crops: Mango (Mangifera indica), Citrus spp., Litchi (Litchi chinensis), Guava (Psidium guajava), Protected Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
cards.notes: Essential for micro-irrigation scheduling and high-density orchard canopy architecture.
cards.etymology: From Greek οἶκος ('oikos', dwelling/house) + φυσιολογία ('physiologia', natural science, from 'physis' nature + 'logos' discourse); coined by Eugenius Warming (1902) to bridge ecological plant geography with functional botany.
cards.synonyms: physiological ecology, environmental plant physiology
cards.see_also: stomatal conductance, water-use efficiency, vapor pressure deficit, abiotic stress, photosynthesis, chlorophyll fluorescence

cards.biological_mechanism: The genetically determined architecture and spatial ontogeny of flowering, defined by whether floral buds develop terminally or laterally, and whether blooms are produced on current season herbaceous shoots, 1-year-old dormant twigs, or specialized perennial spur systems (short shoots). Governed by meristem fate genes (e.g. TERMINAL FLOWER 1 / TFL1 and APETALA1 / AP1).
cards.horticultural_practice: Directs commercial canopy pruning, training systems, and pinching. In fruit trees, distinguishing spur-bearers (e.g. spur-type apples on 2+ year wood) from tip-bearers (e.g. Rome Beauty apples or terminal panicle bearing in mango) is critical; pruning tip-bearers as spur-bearers removes all fruiting wood. In floriculture (roses, chrysanthemums), pinching alters apical dominance to modify floral habit from solitary standard blooms to spray sprays.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Floral habit is NOT floral morphology! Morphology describes the internal anatomical structure of single flowers (sepals, petals, stamens, carpels); Floral habit describes the spatial arrangement and shoot age where floral buds are produced across the canopy architecture.
cards.key_crops: Malus domestica (Apple spur vs tip types), Mangifera indica (Terminal panicles), Rosa chinensis (Standard vs spray habit), Chrysanthemum morifolium
cards.notes: Pruning rule: Never head back shoot tips of terminal tip-bearing cultivars during the dormant season.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'flos'/'floris' (flower) + Latin 'habitus' (condition, bodily appearance, character, from 'habere' to have or hold).
cards.synonyms: flowering habit, bearing habit, bloom pattern, inflorescence habit
cards.see_also: spur-bearing, tip-bearing, inflorescence, terminal bud, pruning, canopy architecture

cards.biological_mechanism: The biochemical and physiological commitment of a vegetative shoot apical meristem (SAM) to switch from vegetative plastochrons to reproductive morphogenesis. Mediated by systemic synthesis of the mobile protein FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT / florigen) in leaves, which translocates via phloem to the SAM, interacts with the bZIP transcription factor FD, and upregulates floral identity genes (AP1, LFY) while suppressing vegetative genes (TFL1).
cards.horticultural_practice: Manipulated in orchards via low-temperature vernalization, water stress, or chemical growth regulators. In mango (Mangifera indica), paclobutrazol (Cultar) is applied to the soil to inhibit gibberellin biosynthesis (since gibberellins strongly repress floral induction), promoting winter flowering. In litchi, girdling or water withholding in autumn blocks vegetative flushing and promotes induction.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT confuse Floral Induction with Floral Initiation / Differentiation! Floral induction is the physiological, invisible biochemical trigger (FT/gibberellin balance); Floral initiation is the subsequent anatomical, microscopic differentiation of sepal/petal primordia at the shoot apex.
cards.key_crops: Mangifera indica (Mango), Litchi chinensis (Litchi), Citrus spp., Chrysanthemum morifolium, Malus domestica
cards.notes: Rule of thumb: High gibberellin synthesis in seeds or young leaves is the primary antagonist of floral induction in woody fruit trees.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'flos'/'floris' (flower) + Latin 'inductio' (a leading into, from 'in-' + 'ducere' to lead); coined to contrast internal signaling with physical evocation.
cards.synonyms: floral evocation, reproductive evocation, flower induction
cards.see_also: floral initiation, florigen, flowering locus t (ft), vernalization, photoperiodism, alternate bearing

cards.biological_mechanism: The reproductive ontogenetic phase characterized by petal expansion, anthesis (opening of flower buds), anther dehiscence, pollen viability, stigma receptivity, and fertilization. Governed by ethylene sensitivity, auxin gradients, and rapid cellular water influx into petal vacuoles. Represents the peak vulnerability window to temperature extremes and desiccation.
cards.horticultural_practice: In commercial greenhouse floriculture (cut roses, gerberas, liliums, orchids), day/night temperatures, relative humidity (60-70%), and photoperiod are regulated to schedule uniform anthesis for target festival markets. Anti-ethylene treatments (STS - silver thiosulfate, 1-MCP) are applied immediately prior to or during flower harvesting to delay petal senescence.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Anthesis is specifically the act of flower opening and anther dehiscence; the Flowering Phase encompasses the entire receptive bloom window from anthesis to fertilization and petal wilting.
cards.key_crops: Rosa chinensis (Cut rose), Chrysanthemum morifolium, Lilium longiflorum, Gerbera jamesonii, Mangifera indica
cards.notes: High temperature or rainfall during anthesis causes pollen wash-off, desiccation, and poor fruit set.
cards.etymology: From Middle English 'flour' (from Old French 'flor'/'flour', from Latin 'flos') + Greek φάσις ('phasis', an appearance, phase of celestial bodies, from 'phainein' to appear).
cards.synonyms: anthesis, bloom stage, floral stage, blooming period
cards.see_also: anthesis, pollination, floral induction, stigma receptivity, vase life, phenology

cards.biological_mechanism: A synchronized, episodic wave of rapid shoot elongation and leaf expansion or panicle bud emergence originating from previously quiescent or resting terminal meristems, alternating with intervals of apical bud quiescence in woody perennial plants. Regulated by endogenous hormonal balances—specifically root-derived cytokinin surges and declining gibberellin levels signaling bud burst.
cards.horticultural_practice: In commercial mango (Mangifera indica) and litchi (Litchi chinensis) orchards, growers stimulate 1-2 vegetative flushes immediately post-harvest through canopy pruning and nitrogenous fertilization. Subsequent autumn vegetative flushes are chemically suppressed using paclobutrazol (Cultar - a gibberellin biosynthesis inhibitor) alongside regulated deficit irrigation to ensure synchronized, heavy floral panicle flushes in winter.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT confuse tropical rhythmic flushing with continuous temperate spring shoot growth! In subtropical fruit trees like mango and litchi, late autumn vegetative flushes act as strong gibberellin sinks and sources that directly antagonize floral evocation (flush-flower antagonism). Paclobutrazol suppresses vegetative flushes to allow floral flushes to proceed.
cards.key_crops: Mango (Mangifera indica), Litchi (Litchi chinensis), Citrus spp., Tea (Camellia sinensis), Cacao (Theobroma cacao)
cards.notes: Core physiological determinant of alternate bearing and floral induction in mango and litchi.
cards.etymology: From Middle English 'flusschen' (to fly up suddenly) and Old French 'flus' (a sudden surge/flow), derived from Latin 'fluere' (to flow); applied to the sudden, visible surge of new green shoots.
cards.synonyms: vegetative flush, episodic growth, shoot emergence
cards.see_also: bud dormancy, paclobutrazol, panicle initiation, alternate bearing, apical dominance, phenology

cards.biological_mechanism: A specialized macroscopic, multicellular epigeous or hypogeous reproductive organ (sporocarp / basidiocarp / ascocarp) developed from densely interwoven dikaryotic vegetative hyphae. It differentiates into specialized tissues (pileus, stipe, lamellae/gills) bearing the meiotic hymenium where basidia produce and forcibly discharge millions of haploid basidiospores.
cards.horticultural_practice: In commercial edible mushroom farming (Pleurotus ostreatus, Agaricus bisporus, Volvariella volvacea), mushroom houses maintain vegetative mycelial run in darkness at 24-28°C and >85% CO2. Once substrate is colonized, growers induce fruiting body initiation (pinning) by a cold shock (drop of 4-6°C), introducing fresh air (CO2 < 1000 ppm), ambient light (500-1000 lux), and 85-90% relative humidity.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT confuse fruiting bodies with botanical fruits! A botanical fruit (fructus/pericarp) is exclusively an angiosperm ovary containing seeds. In horticulture, fruiting body is strictly a mycological sporocarp (mushroom), NEVER a tree branch, spur, or pome fruit!
cards.key_crops: Pleurotus ostreatus (Oyster mushroom), Agaricus bisporus (Button mushroom), Volvariella volvacea (Paddy straw mushroom), Lentinula edodes (Shiitake)
cards.notes: Pinning requires a sharp environmental shift: drop in temperature and CO2, coupled with light exposure.
cards.etymology: Compound from Latin 'fructus' (produce, fruit) + Old English 'bodig' (vessel, form); specialized in mycology to denote macroscopic spore-bearing structures.
cards.synonyms: sporocarp, basidiocarp, ascocarp, mushroom
cards.see_also: spawn culture, mycelium, basidiospore, pinning, casing soil, Pleurotus ostreatus

cards.biological_mechanism: The total physical biological repository of genetic material—including hereditary alleles, structural genes, and epigenetic variations—preserved as viable totipotent entities (seeds, meristem cultures, pollen, or cryopreserved shoot tips).
cards.horticultural_practice: Ex situ conservation in gene banks at -18°C (orthodox seeds) or in liquid nitrogen (-196°C cryopreservation for recalcitrant horticultural species like mango and jackfruit), systematically evaluated for biotic/abiotic stress alleles for pre-breeding introgression.
cards.exam_trap: Distinguish between Gene Pool and Germplasm: Gene Pool is an abstract, theoretical concept describing all genes in an interbreeding population; Germplasm refers to the physical, tangible biological samples (accessions) conserved in storage or fields.
cards.key_crops: Solanum spp. (wild tomato/potato relatives), Malus domestica, Musa spp., Mangifera indica
cards.notes: Primary source for introgressing Late Blight and Bacterial Wilt resistance genes.
cards.etymology: Coined in 1883 by German biologist August Weismann as 'Keimplasma' (from Latin 'germen', bud or sprout, and Greek πλάσμα, 'plasma', something formed or molded).
cards.synonyms: genetic resources, hereditary material, gene pool
cards.see_also: gene bank, landrace, accession, cryopreservation, inbred lines

cards.biological_mechanism: Wound-healing cascade: necrotic cell layer forms and dissolves; unspecialized wound-repair callus proliferates from vascular cambium of both stock and scion, interlocks in the graft zone, and subsequently redifferentiates into continuous vascular cambium, xylem vessels, and phloem sieve elements.
cards.horticultural_practice: Whip-and-tongue, veneer, or cleft grafting conducted during active sap movement. Requires intimate cambial alignment, sharp clean incisions, structural binding with grafting tape, and waterproofing with wax to prevent desiccation.
cards.exam_trap: Vascular cambium must make direct physical contact along at least one full side. Callus can bridge microscopic gaps, but misaligned or dead cambia result in anatomical rejection or delayed structural failure (delayed incompatibility).
cards.key_crops: Mango (Mangifera indica), Apple (Malus domestica), Citrus spp., Grafted Tomato/Eggplant (rootstock resistance)
cards.notes: Used widely for dwarfing rootstocks in intensive orchards and nematode resistance in solanaceous vegetables.
cards.etymology: From Middle English 'graff'/'graft', from Old French 'graffe' (grafting tool, stylus), derived via Latin 'graphium' from Ancient Greek γραφεῖον (grapheion, 'stylus' or 'writing implement', describing the pencil-like tapered shape of a prepared scion).
cards.synonyms: graftage, top-working
cards.see_also: scion, rootstock, graft union, callus tissue, vascular cambium, graft incompatibility

cards.biological_mechanism: The scientific discipline and applied bio-industry dedicated to the intensive cultivation, propagation, genetic improvement, canopy architecture, and postharvest physiology of high-value crops (fruits, vegetables, ornamentals, spices, and plantation species). Fundamentally distinguished from extensive agronomy by intensive individual plant care, high input-output value per unit land area, and high commodity perishability.
cards.horticultural_practice: Encompasses precision protected cultivation (greenhouses/polyhouses), high-density planting (HDP) systems, in-vitro micropropagation, dwarf rootstock manipulation, controlled atmosphere (CA) postharvest storage, and precision fertigation to optimize qualitative traits (sugars, nutraceutical antioxidants, shelf-life, aesthetics).
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Horticulture is NOT synonymous with general agriculture or gardening! Gardening is domestic and non-commercial; Agriculture is the broad umbrella encompassing field crops and livestock; Horticulture is the specialized science of high-value intensive crops divided into Pomology, Olericulture, Floriculture, and Postharvest Technology.
cards.key_crops: Mangifera indica, Solanum lycopersicum, Rosa chinensis, Litchi chinensis, Allium cepa
cards.notes: Primary subdivisions: Pomology (fruits), Olericulture (vegetables), Floriculture & Landscape Hort, and Postharvest Technology.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'hortus' (garden, enclosed plot) + 'cultura' (cultivation, tillage, from 'colere' to till/care for); coined in 17th-century agricultural literature (Peter Lauremberg 1631, Edward Phillips 1678).
cards.synonyms: garden cultivation, high-value crop science, intensive horticultural cultivation
cards.see_also: pomology, olericulture, floriculture, plant propagation, postharvest physiology, agronomy

cards.subfield: Horticultural Plant Biotechnology / In Vitro Culture
cards.biological_mechanism: An authenticated, axenic, genetically stable primary culture of totipotent plant explants or pure fungal mycelium preserved under minimal subculture intervals. Serves as the genetic and physiological reference standard to derive daughter multiplication cycles, minimizing epigenetic drift, somaclonal mutations, and pathogen accumulation.
cards.horticultural_practice: In plant micropropagation (e.g. virus-free potato, strawberry, banana), mother cultures are initiated from meristem tip culture (0.2-0.5 mm to exclude viruses), confirmed disease-free via ELISA/PCR, and conserved at low temperature (18-20°C) with reduced osmotic media. In mushroom production, mother cultures are maintained on slant agar tubes (PDA) to inoculate mother spawn bottles.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Mother cultures should NEVER be subcultured indefinitely! In commercial micropropagation, passages from a mother culture are strictly limited to 5-8 subcultures to prevent somaclonal variation, vitrification (hyperhydricity), or loss of vigor.
cards.key_crops: Musa spp. (Banana cv. Grand Naine), Solanum tuberosum (Potato seed stock), Fragaria × ananassa (Strawberry), Pleurotus ostreatus (Mother spawn source)
cards.notes: Always verify genetic purity and freedom from systemic latent viruses before scaling daughter cultures.
cards.etymology: Compound from Middle English 'moder' (from Old English 'mōdor') + Latin 'cultura' (tillage, cultivation, from 'colere'); adapted in modern in-vitro technology to designate the ancestral, pure clonal repository.
cards.synonyms: master culture, foundation stock, axenic stock culture, primary culture
cards.see_also: subculture, tissue culture, explant, somaclonal variation, axenic culture, spawn culture

cards.biological_mechanism: An endogenous developmental abscission cascade whereby woody fruit trees self-regulate excessive crop load post-fertilization. Triggered by intense intra-canopy competition for non-structural carbohydrates (sucrose/hexoses) among growing fruitlet sinks, resulting in reduced polar auxin transport (IAA) from young embryos through the pedicel. The drop in auxin sensitivity permits ethylene and abscisic acid (ABA) to activate cellulase and polygalacturonase in the pedicel abscission zone, causing clean fruitlet detachment.
cards.horticultural_practice: Occurs in distinct waves: first drop (unpollinated/defective flowers), post-bloom drop (fertilized weak fruitlets), and June drop (mid-season drop of developing fruits due to carbohydrate stress). Commercial orchardists monitor natural drop before deciding on supplementary chemical thinners (NAA, carbaryl, ethephon) or hand thinning to reach target leaf-to-fruit ratios (e.g. 30-40 leaves per fruit in apples).
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Natural thinning is a self-regulating, autonomous physiological response; Hand/Chemical thinning is intentional human intervention. Natural thinning alone is frequently INSUFFICIENT in cultivars prone to alternate bearing (e.g. Fuji apples or Langra mangoes), requiring orchardists to thin further.
cards.key_crops: Malus domestica (Apple - June drop), Mangifera indica (Mango - 99% fruitlet drop), Citrus sinensis (Citrus post-bloom drop), Prunus persica (Peach)
cards.notes: Over 99% of initiated mango flowers naturally drop; only 0.1-0.5% reach harvestable maturity.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'naturalis' (by birth, innate, in accord with nature) + Middle English 'thynnen' (from Old English 'þynnian', to make thin or sparse, from 'þynne' thin).
cards.synonyms: physiological fruit drop, self-thinning, June drop, fruitlet abscission
cards.see_also: abscission zone, crop load, overbearing, chemical thinning, sink strength, auxin transport

cards.biological_mechanism: Capacity to tolerate severe maturation desiccation down to 2–5% moisture content and prolonged storage at sub-zero temperatures (-18°C to -20°C). Mediated by accumulation of Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA) proteins, sucrose/raffinose oligosaccharide vitrification (cytoplasmic glass formation), and metabolic arrest preventing membrane collapse.
cards.horticultural_practice: Seeds of vegetable crops (tomato, cabbage, onion, carrot) are dried in dehumidified drying rooms (15–20% RH, 15°C–20°C) down to 5–6% moisture content, hermetically sealed in laminated foil packets, and stored in medium-term (4°C) or long-term base collections (-18°C).
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Orthodox seeds do NOT require dormancy to be orthodox! Many orthodox seeds are non-dormant upon drying (e.g. tomato, pea, onion). Longevity is quantitatively predictable by Roberts seed viability equations.
cards.key_crops: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), Onion (Allium cepa), Cabbage (Brassica oleracea), Pea (Pisum sativum)
cards.notes: Adheres strictly to Roberts seed viability equations.
cards.etymology: From Greek ὀρθός ('orthos', correct/standard) and δόξα ('doxa', opinion/doctrine); formalized in seed biology by E.H. Roberts in 1973.
cards.synonyms: desiccation-tolerant seed
cards.see_also: recalcitrant seed, intermediate seed, seed vigor, cryopreservation, Roberts viability equation

cards.biological_mechanism: The physiological imbalance wherein an excessively high fruit-to-leaf ratio sets on a tree, causing acute carbon exhaustion. The developing embryos of the heavy crop synthesize copious amounts of gibberellins (GA4/GA7), which move basipetally into adjacent bourse or terminal buds, directly repressing the expression of floral evocation genes. Simultaneously, root carbohydrate starvation restricts cytokinin synthesis, triggering complete vegetative/floral bud dormancy and ensuring an OFF year in the subsequent season (alternate bearing).
cards.horticultural_practice: Managed via rigorous early-season crop load control. Orchardists perform chemical thinning (NAA at 10-15 ppm, NAD, BA, or metamitron) at petal fall or 10 mm fruitlet diameter, followed by hand thinning to establish a balanced crop load (typically 1 fruit per cluster or 5-6 fruits per cm2 trunk cross-sectional area). Pruning during the dormant season reduces excessive spur density.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Overbearing and overcropping are synonymous terms for the same physiological defect! Do NOT confuse overbearing with biennial bearing: overbearing is the acute cause (excessive crop load in the ON year); biennial bearing is the chronic multi-year symptom of fluctuating ON and OFF cycles.
cards.key_crops: Malus domestica (Apple cultivars Fuji, Honeycrisp), Mangifera indica (Mango Langra, Amrapali), Citrus reticulata (Mandarin), Pistacia vera (Pistachio)
cards.notes: Key rule: Heavy crop load inhibits return bloom via seed-derived gibberellin synthesis, NOT just carbohydrate depletion.
cards.etymology: Compound from Old English 'ofer' (over, excessive) + 'beran' (to bear fruit, produce, carry, from Proto-Germanic '*beraną'); documented in arboricultural treatises since 1572.
cards.synonyms: overcropping, excessive crop load, biennial bearing trigger
cards.see_also: alternate bearing, fruit thinning, crop load, june drop, gibberellin inhibition, sink-source balance

cards.biological_mechanism: An in vitro biological system containing solely a single target clonal genotype or taxonomic taxon (microorganism, fungal strain, or dedifferentiated plant cell line), rigorously free from all living extraneous symbiotic, commensal, or parasitic contaminants. Crucial for reproducible biochemical assays, Agrobacterium-mediated genetic transformation, and somatic embryogenesis.
cards.horticultural_practice: Maintained using aseptic techniques in class II laminar airflow cabinets with HEPA filtration (99.97% efficiency at 0.3 µm). Explants (shoot tips, nodal segments) undergo multi-step chemical surface sterilization (70% ethanol for 30s followed by 0.1% HgCl2 or 1-2% NaOCl with Tween-20 surfactant) and are checked on nutrient broth to ensure complete axenic status.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Pure culture vs Axenic culture vs Monoxenic culture: A pure culture or axenic culture contains exactly ONE species. Monoxenic culture contains a single target organism growing on a single known living host species (e.g. an obligate biotrophic powdery mildew on host tissue).
cards.key_crops: Solanum tuberosum (Micropropagation), Nicotiana tabacum (Transformation models), Ralstonia solanacearum (Bacterial wilt isolates), Fusarium oxysporum (Wilt screening)
cards.notes: Pioneered by Robert Koch in 1881; the fundamental cornerstone of modern plant biotechnology and phytopathology.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'purus' (clean, unmixed, untainted) + Latin 'cultura' (cultivation, tillage); methodologically established by Robert Koch using agar solid media.
cards.synonyms: axenic culture, monoxenic culture, isolated clone
cards.see_also: axenic, explant, tissue culture, surface sterilization, Koch postulates, contamination

cards.biological_mechanism: Desiccation and chilling intolerance: seeds undergo no maturation drying, are shed at high moisture contents (30–60%), remain metabolically active, and lack protective LEA proteins and oligosaccharide glass vitrification, causing lethal membrane rupture, organelle disorganization, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) damage upon dehydration below 15–30%.
cards.horticultural_practice: Recalcitrant seeds cannot be stored in standard seed banks. Sown immediately in nursery beds or moist sphagnum moss. Long-term conservation requires in-vitro cryopreservation of excised embryonic axes in liquid nitrogen (-196°C) or living field gene banks.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT freeze or dry recalcitrant seeds—freezing causes intracellular ice crystals, and drying causes mechanical tension collapse. Desiccation sensitivity is due to active metabolism and lack of LEA vitrification, NOT high lipid content!
cards.key_crops: Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), Mango (Mangifera indica), Litchi (Litchi chinensis), Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis), Cocoa (Theobroma cacao)
cards.notes: Must be preserved as living plants or cryopreserved embryonic axes.
cards.etymology: From Latin 'recalcitrare' (to kick back or rebel, from 're-' back + 'calcitrare' to kick, from 'calx' heel); classified by E.H. Roberts (1973).
cards.synonyms: desiccation-sensitive seed, non-orthodox seed
cards.see_also: orthodox seed, intermediate seed, embryonic axes, cryopreservation, LEA proteins, chilling injury

cards.biological_mechanism: The sterile carrier substrate (autoclaved whole cereal grains such as wheat, rye, millet, or sawdust) fully permeated and colonized by pure vegetative dikaryotic mycelium of a verified macrofungus strain. Serves as the planting inoculum (the mycological equivalent of seed) to inoculate pasteurized bulk substrates (straw, sawdust, compost) without competition from weed molds.
cards.horticultural_practice: Commercial spawn production in Bangladesh involves soaking wheat or paddy grain overnight, boiling until tender (without bursting the seed coat), mixing with 2% CaCO3 (calcium carbonate) and 2% CaSO4 (gypsum) to prevent clumping and buffer pH, bottling in heat-resistant polypropylene bags, autoclaving at 121°C (15 psi) for 90 minutes, and aseptically inoculating with mother mycelium.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Spawn is NOT grown from fungal spores for commercial production! Spores are products of sexual meiosis that segregate genetically, resulting in unpredictable yield, wild morphology, and degeneration. Commercial spawn is strictly propagated VEGETATIVELY from dikaryotic mycelial master cultures.
cards.key_crops: Pleurotus ostreatus (Oyster mushroom grain spawn), Agaricus bisporus (Button mushroom rye spawn), Volvariella volvacea (Paddy straw spawn)
cards.notes: Spawn quality criteria: Uniform pure white mycelium, fresh mushroom aroma, zero sectoring or dark mold contamination.
cards.etymology: From Anglo-French 'espaundre' / Old French 'espandre' (to scatter, pour out, spread, from Latin 'expandere') + Latin 'cultura'; historically used for fish eggs and adapted in horticulture for mycelial propagation units.
cards.synonyms: mushroom spawn, grain spawn, vegetative inoculum, planting spawn
cards.see_also: mother culture, mycelium, Agaricus bisporus, Pleurotus ostreatus, substrate pasteurization

cards.biological_mechanism: The strategic over-allocation of experimental units, border trees, or replication specimens beyond the minimal effective sample size (n) required by statistical power calculations. In perennial horticultural crops and physiological field experiments, surplus units serve to absorb destructive physiological sampling (e.g. leaf water potential, dry biomass, root scans), border effects, microclimatic edge gradients, and unexpected pest/pathogen mortality.
cards.horticultural_practice: In field trials (e.g. Randomized Complete Block Design - RCBD with tree fruits or vegetables), guard rows (border rows) surrounding each net plot are incorporated as designated surplus. Measurements are taken exclusively from internal net plot trees, while destructive tissue sampling or leaf nutrient analysis is directed to designated surplus trees to prevent canopy disturbance of net measurement plants.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Surplus in agricultural research is NOT waste or redundancy! Failing to incorporate surplus plants forces researchers to either destructively sample from net measurement trees (biasing cumulative yield data) or suffer loss of degrees of freedom in ANOVA when plants die.
cards.key_crops: Mangifera indica (Orchard trial layout), Solanum lycopersicum (Protected greenhouse trials), Brassica oleracea (Field spacing trials)
cards.notes: Net plot vs Gross plot: Gross plot includes surplus guard rows; Net plot contains exclusively harvest measurement plants.
cards.etymology: From Old French 'surplus' (excess, remainder), from Medieval Latin 'superplus' (from Latin 'super', over/above + 'plus', more); completely unrelated to Latin supellex (furniture).
cards.synonyms: buffer units, guard-row surplus, sampling reserve, oversampling allowance
cards.see_also: guard row, border effect, destructive sampling, statistical power, randomized complete block design

cards.biological_mechanism: A single scion shield bud containing active meristem and minimal xylem/bark is inserted under the bark flaps of a vigorous rootstock; callus develops from the rootstock cambium and the scion shield, establishing vascular continuity to the bud trace within 2 to 3 weeks.
cards.horticultural_practice: Conducted in late summer or spring when rootstock cambium is vigorously dividing and bark slips easily without tearing. A vertical cut (2.5 cm) and horizontal cut form a T; flaps are lifted, shield bud inserted, and bound with budding tape leaving the eye exposed.
cards.exam_trap: Prerequisite condition: Bark MUST be slipping (active cambial division). If bark does not slip (dormant season or water stress), T-budding will fail; Chip Budding must be used instead because chip budding does not require bark separation.
cards.key_crops: Citrus (Sweet orange, Mandarin on Rangpur lime), Rose (Rosa spp.), Peach and Plum (Prunus spp.)
cards.notes: Standard commercial propagation technique for citrus nursery stock in Bangladesh.
cards.etymology: Named directly after the shape of the vertical and horizontal cuts forming a 'T' in the rootstock bark; combined with 'budding' (from Middle English 'budde', of Germanic origin).
cards.synonyms: shield budding, T-grafting
cards.see_also: chip budding, rootstock, scion, vascular cambium, bark slipping

cards.biological_mechanism: A genuine botanical seed containing a zygotic embryo and storage tissue (endosperm or cotyledons) enclosed in a protective seed coat (testa), originating from the double fertilization of an ovule in the ovary. Genetically distinct from the maternal vegetative tissues.
cards.horticultural_practice: Adoption of True Potato Seed (TPS) in subtropical vegetable farming: 100–150 g of TPS replaces 2–2.5 metric tons of bulky vegetative seed tubers per hectare, eliminating seed-tuber viral degeneration and slashing storage/freight costs.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: True seed does NOT have to come from two parents—in autogamous crops (tomato, pea), self-pollination produces true seed. The term is specifically used in horticultural production to contrast true botanical seeds with vegetative propagules (potato tubers, garlic cloves, onion sets, bulbils).
cards.key_crops: Potato (Solanum tuberosum - TPS), Onion (Allium cepa), Garlic (Allium sativum - true seed breeding lines)
cards.notes: Essential distinction in potato and allium production.
cards.etymology: Middle English 'trewe' (genuine, authentic) + Old English 'sǣd' (seed, what is sown).
cards.synonyms: botanical seed
cards.see_also: True Potato Seed (TPS), vegetative propagule, seed tuber, seed piece, apomixis

cards.biological_mechanism: Stable epigenetic silencing of floral repressor genes (e.g. FLC - Flowering Locus C in Brassicaceae) via histone modification (H3K27me3) triggered by prolonged non-freezing low temperatures (1°C to 7°C), rendering the shoot apical meristem competent to initiate floral evocation upon subsequent warm/inductive photoperiods.
cards.horticultural_practice: Controlled artificial chilling of hydrated seeds or overwintering stecklings of biennial horticultural crops to synchronize uniform bolting and flowering for hybrid seed production.
cards.exam_trap: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Do NOT confuse vernalization with stratification! Vernalization induces meristematic competence to flower (vegetative-to-reproductive transition); Stratification breaks seed embryo dormancy to allow germination. High temperatures immediately following chilling cause de-vernalization.
cards.key_crops: Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata), Carrot (Daucus carota), Onion (Allium cepa), Beetroot (Beta vulgaris)
cards.notes: Crucial concept for winter vegetable seed production in subtropical zones.
cards.etymology: Coined from Neo-Latin 'vernalizatio' (from Latin 'vernalis', of spring, from 'ver', spring), introduced as a translation of the Russian agricultural term 'yarovizatsiya' (from Slavic 'Yarilo', god of spring).
cards.synonyms: yarovization (historical), low-temperature floral induction
cards.see_also: photoperiodism, chilling requirement, bolting, devernalization, flowering locus c
